source.title: On the Escaping Efficiency of Distributed Adversarial Training Algorithms
source.authors: Ying Cao; Kun Yuan; Ali H. Sayed

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; the supplied text has flattened tables and figure descriptions.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how distributed adversarial training strategy, batch size, graph structure, and perturbation strength affect flatness, clean accuracy, robust accuracy, and training error in image classifiers. This extends generalization and flatness comparisons to adversarial, multi-agent training.
record.gate_note: Own results compare centralized, consensus, and diffusion adversarial training and report model flatness, clean/robust accuracy, and training error. The paper does not test memorization of random labels, interpolation-threshold width sweeps, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, adaptive optimizers, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gap, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The centralized baselines in Tables VI and VIII permit an overlooked V5 comparison: K=8 versus K=16 at local batch 128 gives global batches 1024 versus 2048. Table IV specifies the same 350 epochs and learning-rate milestones for these settings. Held-out results therefore bear on V5 in adversarial training. Distributed-method comparisons and flatness visualizations do not themselves test V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's main paraphrase is accurate: the local finite-horizon theory favors faster escape and flatter decentralized solutions with sufficiently small perturbations and large batches; stronger attacks can break the flatness ordering. Main experiments show decentralized accuracy advantages, with optimization quality helping explain better accuracy despite sharper landscapes. The appendix supports a general tendency, not universal superiority.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares distributed adversarial training algorithms in a multi-agent robust-risk setting; it does not test the original generalization interventions or measures. Its reported accuracy is clean and adversarial accuracy, not the ordinary held-out generalization gap in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Flatness differences depend on perturbation bound/attack strength: decentralized methods tend to be flatter for ℓ2 128/255 and ℓ∞ 3/255, while this tendency may fail at ℓ∞ 8/255. The theoretical comparison also depends on large batch size, heterogeneous agents, and the graph structure. The simulations vary dataset, local batch size, network size, topology, optimizer, and best versus final checkpoint.

fits_no_version.finding: Decentralized adversarial training generally produces flatter filter-normalized robust-risk landscapes under mild attacks; diffusion can instead be sharper under strong attacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The flatness advantage of decentralized over centralized adversarial training depends on perturbation strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Main-table decentralized models outperform centralized models on clean and AutoAttack accuracy at matching settings; optimizer and TRADES appendix results include exceptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decentralized adversarial training can improve held-out clean and robust accuracy relative to centralized training in large-batch settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Under strong attacks, centralized vanilla SGD has higher training error, while sharper decentralized models can achieve better held-out accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization quality helps explain adversarial-training accuracy differences that flatness alone does not explain.

record.problems: The principal flatness evidence is qualitative landscape visualization rather than a numerical flatness or generalization-gap measure. The experiments use relatively small image datasets and are simulated on a single GPU; the authors note limited computational resources and defer fully distributed system evaluation. Accuracy results are reported without uncertainty estimates. Theoretical results are local and finite-horizon and require small perturbation bounds and sufficiently large batches.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numerical table entries beyond the main Tables I–III were extracted for Appendix G Tables VI–XI because of the 60-row cap and because these are supplementary variants of the same qualitative accuracy result; the paper states they show decentralized methods consistently achieve higher clean and perturbed-data accuracy. Additional figure-only landscapes and training-error plots in Figures 7–22 and 18–21 are summarized where the text gives an explicit outcome; their individual curve values are not numerically recoverable.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out performance versus natural-label generalization.
Width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and effects of tuning or optimizer adaptations.

Small-batch baselines, locating a critical batch size, language models, and controlled tests of longer training, warmup, scaling, or normalization changes. B=128 versus B=256 comparisons change training budgets; decentralized K comparisons also change the communication graph.
Dropout interventions and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, or weight decay.

Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking training–test gaps among similarly well-fitted models, including comparisons with norm and margin measures. Filter-normalized robust-risk plots and held-out accuracy do not establish this relationship.
Removal of highly memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: All existing rows remain linked to none because their recorded comparisons concern distributed strategies or flatness rather than the listed effects. Their cannot_determine states concern the listed versions, not whether the reported strategy differences occurred. V5 verdicts use omitted cross-batch comparisons in the supplied text. No uncertainty estimates establish statistical significance. The study is not an original source of V5.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold and test error under ordinary training.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and effects of learned sparse connectivity or convolutional initialization.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and held-out performance under optimizer tuning.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and the effects of recipe adaptations on the generalization gap.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of the training–test generalization gap, including comparisons to norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing the most memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
